guideSummary.surfnerd: Angourie is a classic New South Wales right-hand point that often ranks among the world's Top 10 waves. It jacks up abruptly over a rock ledge and reels through multiple bending bowl sections and chunky walls, a near-perfect wave that never really lets you relax. The tricky entry and heavy sections mean it rewards experienced surfers who can read each bowl on the fly.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Angourie Point on the North Coast is an exposed point break that has quite reliable surf Offshore winds are from the southwest. Waves just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells and the best swell direction is from the east northeast. Sometimes crowded. Take care of rocks, sharks and locals.

It has a punchy, Duranbah-like feel over sand, and it holds more size than the town beaches to the north like Shelly and Angel, which pick up good banks of their own.

A high-tide reef, the Bar Reef, sits at the spot as well.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Black Rock, also known as Aussie Pipe, Wreck Bay, or Summercloud Bay, is one of the hollowest and most photogenic waves in Australia, tucked in beside Jervis Bay and Booderee National Park. It's an intense reefbreak that peels both left and right over a shallow, uneven bottom of cunjevoi and urchins, so there's no margin for error when it's firing. The land here returned to its traditional owners in 1955, and the spot is regarded as the unofficial home of Indigenous surfing.

How the wave behaves depends entirely on the state of the sand, swinging between sucking, vortexing barrels and long, sectioning walls you can slash apart.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Butterbox is a left-hander breaking over a rock ledge on the Long Reef headland. It shares the headland with Little Makaha, a righthand set-up that never quite delivers and sits on oyster and barnacle covered rocks, and with White Rock, a rearing peak that races left towards the exposed shelf.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Caves Beach is a long sand-bottomed beach break in Australia, serving up both lefts and rights along its stretch. The sucking wave peels through a small takeoff zone in front of a swimming pool built onto the ledge. Dee Why beach also holds some good beachbreaks that take a bit more size when the No Mans stretch closes out, plus a kiddies corner tucked behind the pool for something easier.

It's often crowded here. Beware of rocks and locals.

Nasty slabs make this a serious spot best left to experienced surfers.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Duranbah, better known as D-Bah, is one of the world's finest beachbreaks and a powerful, wedging right-hander that breaks over sand. Although it sits on the north side of the Tweed River, it is technically still in New South Wales, with the border running along Boundary St above the north end of the beach. The rivermouth jetties helped shape its hollow peaks, and refraction off the breakwall focuses swell energy onto the main peak, delivering plenty of tube time.

When the surf is up, crowds are likely Watch out for rips, locals and sharks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Evans Head tends to get by-passed, mostly because it's a detour off the Pacific Highway. The breakwall at the rivermouth has its days, throwing rights that stay protected from south winds, though it doesn't break with the power or shape of the Ballina 'Walls'. The curious might find better shape over the backbeach called Chinamans, and there's the rarity of a right point breaking off Snapper Rocks.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Evans Head-Airforce Beach on the North Coast is an exposed beach break that has reasonably consistent surf. Winter is the best time of year for surfing here. The setup runs from the bombie-strewn north end out to the German Bank, which breaks a good mile out to sea, in past the banks in front of the lagoon, and down to high-tide shore breaks partway toward Dee Why. There's a bit of everything here, with both lefts and rights, and it's long been the realm of longboarders and SUPers along with the wind crew who work the outer bombies.

When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Take care of rips and locals.

The take-off zone is spread out and the waves are fairly forgiving, which makes it a calmer, less intense option than the nearby Peak.

guideSummary.surfnerd: North Narrabeen is one of Sydney's most iconic and reliable waves, a sand-bottom beach break firing over a semi-permanent sandbank at the mouth of the Narrabeen Lakes. Long, quality lefts and shorter rights peel across the triangulated bank, and when the sand gets bulldozed from the lake entrance The Alley takes on a rivermouth shape. The rights can be messier and rippy but still pack plenty of punch, while the lefts run down towards the Carpark Rights section, where the wave stacks into a thick, heaving peak over a shallow sandbar that demands skill to avoid the shut-downs.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Pambula Rivermouth is a fast right-hander that peels along a long sandbar where the river meets the sea on Australia's east coast. The barrel is quick and relentless, all speed and no room for turns.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Stockton Beach is a long stretch of sand that arcs for 32 kilometres, so there is almost always some combination of swell and wind working somewhere along it. For most surfers, Birubi Beach at the northern end has the best banks and the easiest access.

Good surf at all stages of the tide. Relatively few surfers here, even on good days. Watch out for urchins, rips, rocks, obstacles, locals and sharks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Burleigh Heads is a right-hand point that peels in front of Pandanus Trees National Park, throwing thick, dredging barrels over sand along a basalt boulder shoreline. It isn't as long as Kirra and the lineup can be more localised, but when the rest of the coast is closed out Burleigh often keeps holding. The setup is split into four sections, Sharkies, The Cove, The Point and Rockbreak, and they rarely all link up, though a single section can offer plenty of tube time when it lines up.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Greenmount is a long, easy right-hand point at the eastern end of Coolangatta beach, where the tree-lined Greenmount Point curls a bank of boulders that the sand sticks to. It has always had a mellow, longboard-friendly feel, and it still shows that heritage today. Since the Tweed River sand-pumping program and the arrival of the 'Superbank', Greenmount's bay and the adjacent Coolangatta Beach have filled with sand and merged into the near-endless Snapper-to-Rainbow lineup.

The beach breaks peel to the right The quality of the surf isn't affected by the tide. Likely to be crowded if working. Be wary of rips - they make surfing here dangerous.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Kawana is a long run of consistent beachbreaks that peel both left and right over sand, with the odd bank stabilised on a rock bottom. The waves can get hollow, and there's a lot of coast to choose from. If a northeast wind is blowing, The Corner up by Point Cartwright is the spot to head for.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Kawana Beach on the North Coast is an exposed beach break that has reasonably consistent surf. Winter is the best time of year for surfing here. Works best in offshore winds from the west northwest. Tends to receive a mix of groundswells and windswells and the optimum swell angle is from the east southeast. Waves at the beach are both lefts and rights. Good surf at all stages of the tide. Sometimes crowded. Take care of Shark protected, rips and jellyfish.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Kings Beach sits just south of town and breaks over a mix of rock ledge and sand. Much of the time it looks messy and forgettable, but it transforms into hollow, pitching peaks when northeast swells arrive. The standout is the KB Groyne at the southern end, which rests on a rock shelf and serves up thick, cylindrical lefts.

The quality of the surf isn't affected by the tide. When it's working here, it can get crowded. Beware of rocks, rips, sharks and jellyfish.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Kirra is a right-hand point that breaks over sand, widely rated as one of the best of its kind anywhere. It is a heavy, barreling wave, with long slabby sections and thick, dredging lips that reward air-drop takeoffs and impossibly deep tubes. Everything here hinges on the sand, and with the ongoing pumping and re-nourishment projects along this stretch, the bank is prone to change.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Kirra on the Gold Coast is a very sheltered point/Groyne break that has fairly consistent surf. Autumn and winter are the favoured times of year for waves. The best wind direction is from the south. Waves just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells and the ideal swell direction is from the southeast. The quality of the surf isn't affected by the tide. Likely to be crowded if working. Watch out for sharks, rips and rocks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Surfers Paradise is a sand-bottomed beachbreak in the middle of the Gold Coast, and the backdrop of hi-rise hotels, casinos and swanky apartment buildings makes it a rare one for Australian waters. The beach itself is dedicated mostly to swimmers, so stay out of the water between the flags — the lifeguards don't have a sense of humour about it. The peaks worth surfing sit in between the patrolled areas, and they swing both ways with lefts and rights.

Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the best swell direction is from the east. Waves at the beach break both left and right. Good surf at all stages of the tide. Often Crowded. Beware of rips, rocks, obstacles, locals and sharks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Bells Beach is Victoria's most famous surf spot, a classic and consistent right-hand point that breaks over a rock ledge. The wave runs long and comes in three sections, starting outside at Rincon, leading into Bell's Bowl, and finishing in the beach shorebreak, and in huge swells those sections can link up into one long ride. Power is the defining trait here: get caught by an outside set and you are in for a flogging and a gruelling paddle back out, especially once it grows beyond double overhead.

Groundswells more frequent than windswells and the optimum swell angle is from the southwest. Best around mid tide when the tide is rising. When it's working here, it can get crowded. Surfing here means negotiating dangerous rips.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Castle Cove is a swell- and wind-exposed bay tucked in below the cliffs, breaking over a patchwork of uneven reef and sand. It's mainly a right-hander, though a left and scattered peaks can show up depending on the swell and how the sand has banked up against the reefs. The bay always runs a good deal bigger than it looks from the clifftop, and the reef serves up abrupt drops, hollow recesses, and fast walls that are prone to closing out.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Castle Cove in Far West Coast is an exposed beach and reef break that has quite consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. The best wind direction is from the northeast. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the best swell direction is from the south. Waves at the beach are both lefts and rights and there are also left and right hand reef breaks on offer.. When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Hazards include rips and rocks.

As the size builds, the sets let you roll in a little further before the wave turns inside-out.

Most days it serves up beginner-friendly, crumbling walls, but when the banks line up it can throw up something much better.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Meanos is the heaviest of the several reefbreaks dotted along Flinders Beach, tucked in beneath the West Head cliffs. It breaks over uneven reef and throws up both lefts and rights. The lefts can be intimidating even at high tide, while the rights come easier, and there's a more forgiving inside reform to fall back on.

Watch out for rocks and sharks.

Groundswells are more common than windswells and the ideal swell direction is from the southwest. A choice of left and right reefs. Best around mid tide when the tide is rising. It's sometimes crowded here. Take care of rips and rocks.

The banks here shift constantly, getting pounded out of shape by big swells and then reforming between storms, so what you find changes from session to session. When the sand lines up you'll get zippy corners, reforms and shorebreak peaks running both left and right.

From the car park lookouts it tends to look smaller than it really is, so it is usually a bit better than expected once you are down at the water.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Torquay Backbeach is a southeast-facing beach that tames southwest swell into easy, rolling rides suited to beginners, longboarders, and just about every kind of craft. Once you're in, the barrel starts grinding straight down the point, wrapping slightly into the bay and rarely letting up long enough for turns, so down-the-line speed is everything.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Margaret River - Southside sits just south of Surfers Point, where a shelf of stone faces into the swell over an uneven reef. It cultivates tubular rights that peel into the channel alongside round, long lefts that close out on the near-dry reef, which can leave you exposed to clean-up sets. Further out, the Bombie is a behemoth peak that barrels left before shouldering off, with a right that stands up and feathers house-size walls into the deep, dark channel.

Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the ideal swell direction is from the west. There is no reef break. Unlikely to be too crowded, even when the surf is up. Beware of urchins, rocks and sharks.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Backdoor is a fierce right-hander tucked into the northern corner of the bay at Cactus, sharing its name and its top-to-bottom barrelling ferocity with the Hawaiian original. It breaks over a sharp, shallow reef that sits close to deep water beneath the cliffs, and the peak is genuinely hard to read. That difficulty keeps it lower on the locals' list, which makes it a rewarding find for a travelling surfer who craves heavy right barrels.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Backdoors in Nullarbor is an exposed reef break that only works once in a while. Winter is the favoured time of year for surfing here. Offshore winds are from the north northeast. Waves just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells and the best swell direction is from the southwest. There is a right hand reef break. Best around low tide. Sometimes crowded. Watch out for rocks, sharks and isolation.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Bullies is a heavy, experts-only right-hand reef break. Extra throaty righthanders drive onto the uneven reef with daunting drops and taut tubes to negotiate, and a thumping shorebreak waits to finish off anyone still standing. The water is always moving around, and a set will hand out a serious thrashing to anyone caught inside.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Bullies in South Australia - East Coast is a fairly exposed beach and reef break that has reasonably consistent surf and can work at any time of the year. The best wind direction is from the north northwest and there is no shelter here from cross shore breezes. Groundswells are more common than windswells and the ideal swell direction is from the south southwest. No beach break here as well as left and right hand reef breaks. Good surf at all stages of the tide. When the surf is up, it can get quite busy in the water. Watch out for dangerous rips.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Cape Kersaint is a heavy, deep-water left-hand pointbreak that peels below cliffs over an uneven reef, and it is not for the faint-hearted. Rumbling walls hurl themselves at the rock shelf, and when a big south swell lands, barrels start to materialise for anyone willing to take on the unpredictable lineup. The surroundings are wild and mostly left to the seals that live around here.
guideSummary.surfForecast: Cape Kersaint in Kangaroo Island is an exposed point break that has reasonably consistent surf. Winter is the optimum time of year for surfing here. Offshore winds blow from the north. Clean groundswells prevail and the ideal swell direction is from the south.The waves is a point break that peels left. Surfable at all stages of the tide. It very rarely gets crowded here. Hazards include rips, rocks and sharks.

It breaks over a shallow rock ledge, and it sits just across a deep, shark-frequented channel. When a decent swell lines up with morning offshores, it can turn into a reeling, world-class barrel with serious volume.

guideSummary.surfnerd: Shipstern Bluff, also known as Fluffys, is one of the world's iconic heavy waves, a right-hand point that breaks over uneven reef just a few metres off a boulder-piled headland in Tasmania. It's regularly mentioned alongside Jaws and Teahupoo for sheer gnarliness. Swells slam abruptly onto the granite ledge, throwing up below-sea-level surges, massive steps in the face, and two-storey double barrels.

It really comes into its own when the outside swell is double-overhead and gets distilled down to a more manageable size on the bank here, which makes it a genuine challenge for average surfers rather than an easy cruise.

The quality of the surf isn't affected by the tide. Even when there are waves, it's not likley to be crowded. Watch out for urchins, rips, rocks, locals and sharks. North Tabourie

guideText.text: Whites Reef in Far West Coast is an exposed reef break that has fairly consistent surf. Winter is the favoured time of year for surfing here. The break needs some west in the swell for it to break and barely start going till there's 3m of swell running . If the swell is south it needs to be huge otherwise it just doesn't get in there. Off shore winds are from the ESE and it can handle any wind from the south if it is light. It can handle any wind strength from the SE-NE because the cliffs provide shelter but as soon as there's to much north or any west it will start to get chopped up. It breaks as a left hander over a slab base and on a good day rides are long to very long. Starts working at 2ft and holds 10+. Good surf at all stages of the tide. Often Crowded. Watch out for rips, rocks and sharks. Whites Reef
